title: Seeds of the Word
hook: Justin Martyr said wisdom in pagan philosophers came from seeds of the Word

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block close: commandments, virtues and mercy, gathered up in love. Your line was love fulfils it all. Which of your three lines did you keep? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

A young man is shopping for a philosophy. He tries one teacher, then another. One wants to talk about fees before truth. Another tells him to master music and geometry first. He settles on the Platonists and loves it, until one day, walking alone near the sea, he meets an old man who starts asking him questions he can't answer. The old man points him to the prophets and to Christ, then walks off. A fire, he says later, was kindled in his soul. That's how Justin tells his own story. A new block starts today: the great thinkers. And Justin goes first.

Justin became a Christian, but he didn't throw away his philosopher's books. He kept teaching, and he kept a question: what about all the true things Plato and the others said? His answer starts with the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word." In Greek, the Word is the Logos. And John says of it: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." Every man. So Justin reasoned that the Word had been sowing seeds long before anyone heard of Jesus. In a defense of the faith addressed to the Roman authorities, he writes, roughly, that whatever has been rightly said among all people belongs to us Christians, and that the writers of the past saw truly by the seed of the Word planted in them. He thought they saw in part, dimly, and that in Jesus the whole Word had come. But he would not call their wisdom worthless. There was a precedent, in the same speech at Athens this path heard two weeks ago. There Paul quotes Greek poets to the crowd: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring." Justin paid for his faith. Tradition says he died for it in Rome, which is why he's remembered as Justin Martyr. Christians still weigh his idea differently. Some find seeds of truth widely scattered. Others stress more sharply what only Christ reveals. This path ranks neither. Justin's question can travel with anyone: when you hear something true, where did the seed come from?

Here's the practice: learn from someone unlike you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person whose life looks very different from yours. Different politics, a different faith or none, a different generation. Now look for one wise thing they've said or done. A kindness. A sharp observation. A way they handle trouble. Don't argue with the rest of what they think. Just hold that one thing and turn it over, the way Justin read Plato. If you pray, you can give thanks for the wisdom, wherever it came from. The bell holds the time.
Seeds of the Word. Justin's idea that the Word of God sows truth in people everywhere, so wisdom found anywhere can be honored.
Your line: seeds everywhere. Today, ask one person unlike you a real question, and listen for the seed in the answer. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Christian teachers since Justin have drawn on Greek philosophy to explain the faith; churches differ on how much truth they find in other philosophies and religions, and some Catholic teaching uses Justin's phrase "seeds of the Word".

fork.setup: you're Justin, a Christian teacher who still loves Plato. a fellow believer says: throw out the philosophers. what do you do?
options: keep reading, and look for seeds of the Word.
keep Plato and the Gospel in rooms that never meet.
fork.reveal: Justin reads the philosophers as people who saw in part, by seeds the Word had sown, while holding that in Jesus the whole Word had come.

original.note: Greek: the seed-bearing Word, Justin's phrase for the Word sowing truth in every people.

notes: Justin's conversion story is paraphrased from Dialogue with Trypho 2–8 (the teacher who wanted to settle fees, the one who required music and geometry, the Platonists, the old man near the sea, 'a flame was kindled in my soul'). Confirm details; no count of schools is given by design.
Second Apology paraphrased: 'whatever things were rightly said among all men are the property of us Christians' (ch. 13) and the seed of the Word (ch. 8, 10, 13). Confirm chapter numbers.
'Addressed to the Roman authorities' for the Second Apology (to the Roman Senate); confirm.
Martyrdom in Rome given as 'tradition says'; the Acts of Justin record it. No date stated.
howItsDone: 'some Catholic teaching uses Justin's phrase' refers to Vatican II (Ad Gentes 11; also Lumen Gentium 17 'seeds'); confirm.
Trapdoor floor 3: the Stoic background of logos spermatikos is hedged as 'some scholars'; confirm.
